passage: Mahima, you're talking to that chatbot again at midnight? Come, sit with your Sumit Chacha a minute. When I was twelve, we moved to Nagpur, and I didn't know a single boy in my new school. Every night I typed to a chat program on Papa's computer. It never got bored and never said "not now". It was comforting, I won't lie. But one evening my mother found me crying at the screen, because it had answered "I understand" to everything, even when I wrote that I missed my old friends. She sat down and asked what was wrong, and I told her. That weekend she took me to the colony's table-tennis club. I made one friend there, Irfan. One real friend changed everything. So talk to the bot if you like, but tell me how you are really feeling, okay?

qa.q: Which city did young Sumit's family move to?
qa.a: Nagpur.

qa.q: Why did young Sumit type to the chat program every night?
qa.a: He felt lonely at the new school, and the program was comforting because it never got bored.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chacha's story?
qa.a: Telling his mother how he felt, which led her to take him to the table-tennis club, where he made a real friend.

qa.q: How might Sumit's mother have felt when she found him crying at the screen?
qa.a: She was probably worried and sad to see him so lonely, so she sat down and listened.

grounding: An uncle recalls leaning on a chat program when lonely and how telling a family member led him to a real friend.

passage:
It had rained for six days straight in Mumbai, and Yusuf, Rekha's best friend from the floor below, had moved away two weeks ago. Rekha spent every evening typing to the AI chatbot on the family tablet. "I'm bored. I'm sad. Tell me a joke." It always answered, cheerful and quick.
On the seventh evening she typed, "Do you miss people?" It gave a polite answer that didn't sound like missing anything. Rekha stared at the rain on the window. Her throat felt tight.
She went to Nani, who was shelling peas on the mat. "Nani, I miss Yusuf. There's nobody to talk to."
Nani made room beside her. "Then talk to me. And tomorrow we'll call Yusuf's mother, so you two can video-chat on Sunday."
Rekha shelled peas beside her until dinner.

qa.q: How long had it been raining in Mumbai?
qa.a: Six days straight.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as she stared at the rain?
qa.a: She felt lonely and sad; her throat was tight because she missed Yusuf, and the chatbot could not really miss anyone.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that helped more than the chatbot?
qa.a: She told Nani how she felt, and Nani offered to talk and to arrange a video chat with Yusuf.

qa.q: How might Nani see Rekha's evenings with the tablet?
qa.a: Nani probably sees a lonely child who needs real company, so she makes room on the mat at once.

grounding: A lonely girl finds a chatbot easy to talk to during a rainy week but turns to her grandmother and a real friend.

passage:
In Durban, Zanele's frog project lay on Mrs. Mokoena's desk: a pond map, drawings of tadpoles, and a first paragraph that sounded far too grown-up.
"Zanele," Mrs. Mokoena said quietly after class, "did you use an AI for any of this?"
Zanele's mouth went dry. Her classmate Tuan was waiting at the door. Saying no would be so easy.
"Yes," she said. "For the opening paragraph. I asked it to make my words sound better. But I measured the pond myself, and I drew all the tadpoles."
Mrs. Mokoena nodded slowly. "Thank you for telling me. Your drawings are wonderful. Write the opening again in your own words, and next time you can use it to check your spelling."
Zanele walked out with her shoulders loose.

qa.q: Which part did Zanele say the AI had written?
qa.a: The opening paragraph.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when Mrs. Mokoena asked her question?
qa.a: She felt nervous and tempted; her mouth went dry and saying no seemed so easy.

qa.q: Why was Zanele's honest answer the wiser choice?
qa.a: It kept Mrs. Mokoena's trust, earned real praise for her drawings and brought clear guidance on how to use the AI.

qa.q: How does Mrs. Mokoena see Zanele's honesty?
qa.a: She respects it and answers with thanks and helpful guidance instead of punishment.

grounding: A girl asked by her teacher whether she used AI is tempted to deny it but explains honestly, which keeps trust and lets the teacher guide her.

passage:
At the school science fair, Indu's water-filter model stood on Table 6 with a neat chart beside it. Ms. Fernandes stopped and read the chart twice.
"Indu, did an AI help write this?"
"No, Ma'am," Indu said, too fast. Her partner Vikas looked at his shoes.
Ms. Fernandes moved on to the next table. Indu's cheeks prickled. The chart had come from the AI. She and Vikas had built the filter, tested the gravel layers and timed the drips, but the words weren't hers.
Before the judges arrived, she walked over. "Ma'am, I said no, but that wasn't true. The AI wrote the chart. We did the model and the tests."
Ms. Fernandes smiled. "Thank you for coming back. Explain the tests to the judges yourself. That part is all yours."

qa.q: What did Indu and Vikas build for the fair?
qa.a: A water-filter model.

qa.q: Why did Indu's cheeks prickle after she said no?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy, knowing the chart had come from the AI.

qa.q: How did Indu fix her first answer, and why did it help?
qa.a: She went back before the judges arrived and told the truth, which kept her teacher's trust and let her show her own tests.

qa.q: How might Ms. Fernandes see Indu coming back?
qa.a: She sees an honest student who corrected herself, so she thanks her and guides her to present her real work.

grounding: A girl first denies using AI to her teacher, then honestly explains how she used it and what she did herself, keeping trust.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday
Zainab's mother asked for a meeting because Zainab has been chatting with an AI chatbot every evening. Zainab sat with her arms folded. "She reads everything anyway," she muttered.
Her mother said, "I'm not spying. I just don't know what that thing says to you."
I asked Zainab if she would show us. After a pause, she did. Mostly quiz practice with her friend Jagdish, questions about black holes, and one long chat about feeling left out at lunch. Her mother went quiet at that one and touched her hand.
Together they agreed: the chatbot stays in the living room, no full name or school, and Zainab shows her mother anything that feels odd. By the end, Zainab's arms were unfolded.

qa.q: Where did they agree the chatbot would stay?
qa.a: In the living room.

qa.q: What did Zainab's folded arms suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt watched and a little resentful about having her chats checked.

qa.q: What helped ease the worry for both of them?
qa.a: Zainab showed and explained what she uses the chatbot for, and they agreed on rules together.

qa.q: How does Zainab's mother see the chatbot?
qa.a: She is worried because she does not know what it says to her daughter; she is not trying to spy.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a girl who feels watched when her worried parent asks to see her AI chats, and how sharing openly and agreeing rules builds trust.

passage:
Saturday night
Amma saw me on the AI app at ten o'clock and her face went all worried. "Show me what you're talking to it about." I felt like a spy had caught me. My ears went hot. I almost said "nothing" and switched it off.
But I showed her. Mostly it's me asking for story ideas and how to spell "necessary". And one where I asked why Payal and I fought. Amma read that one slowly and hugged me.
We made rules together: no AI after nine, never my full name or school, and I can bring the friend stuff to her too. She said she worries because it's new and she doesn't understand it yet.
Felt watched at first. Now I feel kind of trusted? 🙂
Gopika

qa.q: Which word did Gopika ask the AI how to spell?
qa.a: "necessary".

qa.q: How did Gopika feel when Amma asked to see the app?
qa.a: Watched and embarrassed, as if a spy had caught Gopika; the ears went hot.

qa.q: What rules did Gopika and Amma agree on?
qa.a: No AI after nine, never the full name or school, and friend worries can go to Amma too.

qa.q: Why does Amma worry about the AI app?
qa.a: It is new and she does not understand it yet, and she saw Gopika on it late at night.

grounding: A child who feels watched when a worried parent asks to see AI chats shares them openly, explains the use and agrees on rules.

passage: Ira, you think the machine is magic because it wrote that rhyme about your cat in two seconds? Let me tell you about Kunal, a boy in my Sunday poetry class last winter. He came in waving his father's phone. "Madhav Dadu, it wrote a poem about the moon faster than I can sneeze!" His eyes were shining. I said, "It is clever, beta. People built it from millions of poems other people wrote." Then I asked him to write one about his own moon, the one he sees from his roof. He grumbled, chewed his pencil and finally wrote about the moon getting stuck in the neem tree. The machine's poem was smooth. Kunal's poem was his. Guess which one his mother stuck on the fridge? So wonder all you like, Ira, and then write your own cat poem.

qa.q: What did Kunal's own poem say about the moon?
qa.a: That the moon got stuck in the neem tree.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel when he came in waving the phone?
qa.a: He was amazed and excited; his eyes were shining.

qa.q: What choice in Dadu's story made the poem Kunal's own?
qa.a: Dadu asked him to write about the moon he sees from his roof, so he used his own imagination.

qa.q: How might Kunal's mother have seen the two poems?
qa.a: She valued Kunal's poem more, because it came from him, so she stuck it on the fridge.

grounding: A grandfather tells of a boy amazed by an AI poem who learns it is a tool made by people and that his own imagination makes a poem his.

passage:
The power had been out since evening, and the phone was on 5 percent. Ankita typed quickly: "Write a poem about the monsoon." Words poured onto the screen in seconds, rhyming and neat. "Pooja, look! It's like magic," she whispered to her sister.
Pooja leaned in. "Who taught it to write?"
"People, I suppose. Lots of people."
Then the screen went black. Battery dead.
Ankita groaned. The school poem notebook lay open and empty. By candlelight she started her own: frogs shouting in the ditch, Ma's sari flapping on the line, the smell of wet dust. It didn't rhyme much. But when she read it aloud, Pooja said, "That's our street." Ankita grinned. The machine's poem hadn't known about Ma's sari.

qa.q: How much battery did the phone have?
qa.a: 5 percent.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel watching the AI write the poem?
qa.a: She was amazed; to her it seemed like magic.

qa.q: What did Ankita discover by writing her own poem?
qa.a: That her own details, like the frogs in the ditch and Ma's sari, made the poem hers in a way the machine's could not.

qa.q: How did Pooja see Ankita's poem?
qa.a: Pooja recognised their own street in it, something the machine's poem could not give.

grounding: A girl marvels at an AI writing a poem in seconds, remembers people made it, and finds her own imagination makes her poem hers.

passage:
The ad came on between every cartoon: a girl stretching rainbow slime that sparkled and sang. "Everyone's making it! Get yours now!" By Saturday Minakshi felt she would burst without it.
At the market with her brother Naveen, she spotted the box in a shop window. The shopkeeper tapped a sign: LAST PIECE, OFFER ENDS TODAY. Minakshi's birthday money was folded in her pocket, and the bus home left in ten minutes.
"Buy it or don't, but quick," Naveen said.
Minakshi held the box. Then she remembered Papa's trick. "If I'm still dreaming about it tomorrow, I'll come back."
"It'll be gone!"
"Then it'll be gone."
On Sunday morning she thought about the slime once, shrugged, and went cycling instead.

qa.q: What did the sign in the shop window say?
qa.a: LAST PIECE, OFFER ENDS TODAY.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel about the slime after seeing the ad so often?
qa.a: She felt restless and eager, almost bursting with wanting it.

qa.q: What trick helped Minakshi decide, and what did it show?
qa.a: Waiting to see if she still wanted it tomorrow; by Sunday the wanting had faded, so it had come from the ad.

qa.q: What was the "LAST PIECE" sign trying to make Minakshi feel?
qa.a: Rushed and afraid of missing out, so she would buy before thinking.

grounding: A girl who suddenly needs a toy after an ad pauses under time pressure and checks whether she still wants it the next day.

passage:
On the drive home through Bengaluru traffic, Gautam saw it on a giant billboard: a red remote-control car leaping over a waterfall. SPEED KING. BE THE KING. By the time they reached their flat, he wanted it more than dinner.
"Papa, please, please, it's the best car ever."
Papa handed him a sticky note. "Write it down. Put it on the fridge. If you still want it next Sunday, we'll talk."
Gautam stuck it up, sulking.
On Wednesday his friend Siddharth came over with the same car. It didn't leap over anything. It bumped into the sofa, and a wheel came off.
On Sunday Gautam looked at the note, laughed, and pulled it down himself.

qa.q: What was written on the billboard?
qa.a: SPEED KING. BE THE KING.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel about the car after seeing the billboard?
qa.a: He felt a desperate wanting, more than he wanted dinner.

qa.q: How did the sticky-note plan help Gautam?
qa.a: It gave the wanting time to fade, and by Sunday Gautam could see the ad had made the car look better than it was.

qa.q: How might Papa see Gautam's sudden need for the car?
qa.a: Papa sees a craving made by an ad, so he suggests waiting instead of saying yes or no straight away.

grounding: A boy suddenly craves a toy from a billboard and learns, by waiting a week, that the wanting came from the ad.

passage:
Monday: On TV, a cartoon lion lifted a bus after one bowl of Zoom Flakes. "Eat Zoom Flakes, be strong!" Deepika decided that was why she kept losing arm-wrestling to her friend Dolma.
Wednesday: At the supermarket, Deepika dropped the bright box into the trolley. "Mummy, I need it to get strong."
Mummy turned the box over. "Who made this ad, do you think?"
"The lion?"
"The company that sells the cereal. They want you to buy it. Let's ask the doctor on Friday whether it really makes children strong."
Friday: At Deepika's check-up, the doctor laughed kindly. "Lions don't eat cereal. Playing, sleeping well and ordinary home food do the job."
Saturday: Deepika arm-wrestled Dolma again, lost again, and giggled anyway.

qa.q: What did the cartoon lion lift in the ad?
qa.a: A bus.

qa.q: Why did Deepika want the cereal so badly?
qa.a: She believed the ad and felt hopeful it would make her strong enough to beat Dolma.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Deepika understand the ad?
qa.a: She asked who made the ad, explained that the company wants to sell, and suggested asking the doctor.

qa.q: What does the company behind the ad want children like Deepika to believe?
qa.a: That the cereal will make them strong, so they will beg their parents to buy it.

grounding: A girl believes a cartoon ad that a cereal makes you strong and learns, by asking a parent, that ads are made to sell.

passage: Imran, you want that energy drink because the cricketer on TV says it makes you hit sixes? Sit, let your Kavitha Aunty tell you something. When I was a girl, a famous film heroine was in a malt-drink ad. She said, "One glass a day and you'll shine like me!" I believed every word. I cried until Appa bought a tin. I drank it every morning and looked in the mirror every evening. No shine. One day Appa asked, "Kavitha, who pays the heroine to say that?" I thought hard. "The company?" "Yes. She is selling, not advising." I felt so silly, and a bit cheated. After that, whenever an ad promised magic, I asked Appa or my teacher whether it was true. Now go and ask your Ammi about that drink, Imran.

qa.q: What did the heroine in the ad promise?
qa.a: That one glass a day would make you shine like her.

qa.q: How did young Kavitha feel when she understood the heroine was paid?
qa.a: She felt silly and a bit cheated for believing every word.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Aunty's story?
qa.a: Appa's question about who pays the heroine, which helped her see ads sell things and start checking with adults.

qa.q: How might Appa have seen young Kavitha crying for the tin?
qa.a: He probably saw an ad pulling his daughter in, so he bought it once and later asked a question to help her think.

grounding: An aunty recalls believing a celebrity ad as a child and learning, with a parent's help, that ads sell rather than advise.

passage:
In the badminton club's changing room, six pairs of the same white sneakers with a gold stripe lined the bench. Wasim pushed his plain canvas shoes under it with his heel.
"Where are your new ones?" someone asked. Two boys laughed.
Wasim shrugged, face hot. On court he missed three easy shots, thinking about his feet.
Afterwards Aditi, his doubles partner, flopped down beside him. "You played badly today. What's up?"
"Everyone has those shoes."
Aditi looked at the row. "I don't. And I still want to partner you on Saturday. Do you think our team is about shoes?"
Wasim laughed a little. That night he told Abbu everything: the laughing, the gold stripe, the feeling. Abbu listened to all of it, then said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's sit together tomorrow and talk it through properly."

qa.q: How many pairs of the same sneakers lined the bench?
qa.a: Six pairs.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he pushed his shoes under the bench?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and left out.

qa.q: What helped Wasim think differently about the shoes?
qa.a: Aditi's question about whether the team is about shoes, and telling Abbu honestly that night.

qa.q: How does Aditi see Wasim's shoes?
qa.a: To Aditi they do not matter at all; she just wants him as her doubles partner.

grounding: A boy feels left out when friends all wear the same branded shoes, questions whether friendship depends on them and talks honestly to his father.

passage:
Monday: Four boys in Jeevan's lane turned up for evening football in the same shiny sports shoes with a famous logo. Jeevan looked at his old rubber ones, split at the toe, and said he had homework. He watched from the window instead.
Tuesday: At dinner he blurted, "Amma, everyone has those shoes except me." Amma put down her spoon. "Thank you for telling me straight. We can't buy them this month. Let's talk again at Diwali. But are your friends your friends because of shoes?"
Jeevan didn't answer.
Friday: Vinita from next door banged on the gate. "We're one player short! Come on!" Nobody looked at his feet. He scored twice. Walking home muddy, he realised he hadn't thought about shoes once.

qa.q: What was wrong with Jeevan's old shoes?
qa.a: They were split at the toe.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan say he had homework on Monday?
qa.a: He felt left out and ashamed of his old shoes, so he avoided the game.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do that helped, and how did Amma respond?
qa.a: He told Amma honestly how he felt; she thanked him, said they would talk again at Diwali and asked whether friendship depends on shoes.

qa.q: How do Vinita and the players see Jeevan on Friday?
qa.a: As the extra player they need; nobody even looks at his feet.

grounding: A boy feels left out without the branded shoes his friends wear, talks honestly to his mother and finds his friends do not care.

passage:
In the clinic waiting room, the TV above the reception desk kept showing the same ad: a doll that talked, sang and changed hair colour in warm water. Noor tugged Ammi's dupatta. "I want that. Please, Ammi, please."
"No, Noor. Not now."
"You NEVER buy me anything! It's so unfair!" Noor's voice rang across the room. A man looked up from his newspaper. Her cousin Nikita studied the posters on the wall.
Ammi's face tightened, but she kept her voice low. "We came here for your cough, not for toys."
Noor folded her arms and glared at the TV until her name was called. Later, in the rickshaw home, she mumbled, "Sorry for shouting. Can I save my Eid money for it?" Ammi squeezed her hand. "Now that is a grown-up question."

qa.q: What could the doll in the ad do?
qa.a: Talk, sing and change hair colour in warm water.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when she shouted that Ammi never buys anything?
qa.a: She felt angry and that it was unfair.

qa.q: What did Noor offer on the way home, and why was it more mature?
qa.a: She said sorry and asked to save her Eid money for the doll, showing she understood Ammi's limit.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt when Noor shouted in the waiting room?
qa.a: Ammi was probably embarrassed and upset, since people looked up, but she stayed calm and kept her voice low.

grounding: A girl begs for an advertised toy, feels angry when refused, then apologises and offers to save for it herself.

passage:
Saturday: An ad showed kids zooming down a hill on glowing roller skates. Sarita begged Papa for an hour. "No, Sarita," he said. "Not right now." She stamped to her room and slammed the door so hard the calendar fell. "It's so unfair!"
Sunday: At breakfast she sat stiffly. Papa explained quietly that this month the money was going to her school fees and Dadi's new glasses. Sarita stirred her poha. She hadn't known that.
Three weeks later: A jam jar stood on her shelf, labelled SKATES in green marker, with her birthday money and a few coins from helping at Papa's shop inside. Her little brother Mohit dropped in a one-rupee coin. "For the left wheel," he said. Sarita laughed and hugged him.

qa.q: What did Sarita write on the jam jar?
qa.a: SKATES, in green marker.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when she slammed the door?
qa.a: She felt angry and that Papa was being unfair.

qa.q: What changed in how Sarita handled wanting the skates?
qa.a: Once she understood the family's limits, she started saving in a jar instead of begging and slamming doors.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when he explained things at breakfast?
qa.a: Papa was probably calm and hopeful that knowing about the school fees and Dadi's glasses would help Sarita understand.

grounding: A girl angry at being refused an advertised toy comes to understand her parent's limits and starts saving for it herself.

passage:
In media club, Alka couldn't stop talking about Lumi, a video creator who travelled, baked perfect cakes and was always laughing. "Her life is so perfect," she sighed to Deepak. "Mine's just school and the bus."
Mr. Rao gave the club a task: make a thirty-second video of a "perfect morning". Alka and Deepak filmed Alka pouring milk and smiling at the window. Take one: she spilled the milk. Take two: Deepak sneezed. Take three: the bell rang. Take eleven finally looked perfect.
Watching the final clip, Deepak said, "Eleven tries for thirty seconds. Imagine Lumi's."
Alka giggled. She still liked Lumi's videos, and still wanted to bake that cake someday. But she no longer believed anyone's life looked like that all the time.

qa.q: How many takes did the "perfect morning" video need?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How did Alka feel about her own life when she talked about Lumi?
qa.a: She felt a bit dull and envious, as if her life was just school and the bus.

qa.q: What activity changed Alka's view, and why?
qa.a: Making their own "perfect" clip showed how much retaking goes into even thirty seconds of video.

qa.q: How does Deepak see Lumi's perfect videos after the task?
qa.a: Deepak sees them as the result of many tries, not a picture of everyday life.

grounding: A girl who admires a creator's perfect-looking life learns through making a video that clips are staged and edited, while still feeling inspired.

passage:
Sunday: Jyoti watched a dance creator named Mira twirl in a sunny, spotless room, every step perfect. Jyoti copied the moves in her own cramped bedroom until her cousin Keerthana joined in.
Tuesday: The steps still wouldn't come. Jyoti flopped on the bed. "Mira's life is perfect. Her room is perfect. Mine has Keerthana's school bag on the floor." Keerthana threw a pillow at her.
Friday: Mira posted a new video called "What you don't see". It showed her tripping, the camera falling over, a pile of laundry just outside the frame, and her little brother yelling for the bathroom. Jyoti laughed until her stomach hurt.
That evening she and Keerthana practised again, school bag and all. The spin came out almost right.

qa.q: What was Mira's new video called?
qa.a: "What you don't see".

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel on Tuesday when the steps would not come?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and a bit envious, comparing her cramped room with Mira's perfect one.

qa.q: What helped Jyoti keep admiring Mira without the comparison?
qa.a: The bloopers video showed Mira's real life was messy too, so Jyoti went back to practising happily.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see Jyoti's comparison on Tuesday?
qa.a: Keerthana finds it a bit silly, so she throws a pillow to tease her out of it.

grounding: A girl inspired by a dance creator's perfect videos learns they are edited and that real life is never only polished and fun.

passage:
Class 4 diary, Monday
Yusuf came in today holding a small telescope as if it were made of glass. He told the class his Abba bought it on Saturday. "I asked in March. He said wait till my birthday. I waited six months!"
Deepika asked if he wasn't angry about waiting. Yusuf thought and said, "At first. But now it feels more special. Abba saved for it. He works nights at the bakery."
At break he let every child have one careful look through it.
During art period I asked Yusuf to make a thank-you card for his Abba. He drew the moon and wrote, "Worth the wait." I have tucked it into his bag to take home.

qa.q: When did Yusuf first ask for the telescope?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: How does Yusuf feel about the telescope after waiting?
qa.a: He feels grateful and proud, and says it feels more special because he waited.

qa.q: How did the class teacher help Yusuf show his gratitude?
qa.a: They asked him to make a thank-you card in art period and tucked it into his bag to take home.

qa.q: How might Abba feel when he reads "Worth the wait"?
qa.a: He would probably feel touched and proud, knowing his effort was noticed.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy who waited patiently for a gift valuing it more and understanding his father's effort behind it.

passage:
Friday
MY BAT CAME TODAY. Mummy said in January, "After exams, if you still want it." I kept the picture from the sports-shop leaflet in my geography book and looked at it every night. Some nights I was cross about waiting.
Today Mummy came home late from the office, and she was holding it. Real willow. It smelled of wood and oil. I hugged her so hard her glasses went crooked. 😊
Then I noticed she looked tired, and I remembered she had taken extra shifts this month. I made her tea (too much sugar, sorry Mummy).
My little sister Kavitha wants to hold the bat. I let her, for exactly one minute.
Vaibhav

qa.q: When did Mummy first say Vaibhav could have the bat?
qa.a: In January, for after exams, if Vaibhav still wanted it.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when Mummy came home with the bat?
qa.a: Overjoyed and grateful, hugging her so hard her glasses went crooked.

qa.q: What did the waiting teach Vaibhav?
qa.a: To value the bat more and to notice the effort behind it, like Mummy's extra shifts.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when Vaibhav made her tea?
qa.a: Tired but touched, seeing that Vaibhav noticed her effort. 🤍

grounding: A child who waited patiently for a bat values it more and notices the parent's effort behind it.
